the job is to open a shared household account or to help with one entry. that kind of help is not the same as access to a person’s whole private archive.
go the full circle of signing in
save the entry that was actually updated

autofill removes the need to look data up and retype it at every sign-in. but that shortcut has to carry on after the password is changed on the site itself. if the new version stayed only in the form, the next sign-in turns back into a manual search for the value that fits.

saving a new password has to be a visible action. the person sees which entry was updated and can tell a work account from a personal one. if the app requires a manual save, it has to say so clearly while the new value is still available.

an offer to save that comes and goes is especially awkward: a person does not know when they can rely on the familiar step. after a password change there has to be a way at hand to check the entry and sign in again. for a client of your own password file this sequence matters as much as being able to read a compatible format.
understand why the sign-in was refused

a repeating biometric prompt, a sign-in refused on one device and a forgotten main password look alike only from the outside: the vault does not open. the causes and the actions available differ. a person needs to understand their own situation, not press the same button again hoping for a different result.

a login loop on one device and a forgotten main password are different situations. if the same credentials open the vault on a computer, repeating them endlessly on the phone is pointless. the interface has to show at which step the refusal came up and which provided alternatives are available, without suggesting risky actions at random.

with a forgotten main password, what recovery is possible depends on how the vault itself is built and on the owner’s settings. that cannot be replaced with a promise that “we will get everything back”. a person needs to know in advance what is held by them alone and what help can be arranged with a family member. this matters especially for a product with a simple interface: simplicity must not hide the limits of recovery.
move from a warning to an action

a warning about a password is useful when it makes clear what happened to a particular entry. being found in a breach and a strength score are different grounds for attention. a red mark nobody can read leaves a person with anxiety and the extra job of working the terminology out alone.

a strength score needs an explanation separate from a breach notification. one user is surprised that a randomly generated password is judged weak; the review itself does not let you check whether that judgement was sound. the product has to reveal the reason for the mark and tell a recommendation to replace a password apart from information about a particular incident.

a generator becomes useful when the value it offers is saved for the right account and works at the next sign-in. a list of warnings can have an ending just as clear: the person has dealt with a particular entry, not merely opened a red card. a general counter of flags is no substitute for that result.
move access while keeping the contents
test the second step on the new device

a one-time code is usually needed in the middle of a sign-in. so an entry that has vanished or is labelled unclearly stops the whole job, even when the password has been found. what matters is a readable link to the service and the account, and a separate check that the codes are available after the device is replaced.

do not put the password transfer and the second step under one message of success. let the owner sign in to an account of their choice from the new phone and see which confirmation method is in use. the fallback path provided in advance should be explained for that method, without promising one button for every case.

even without a change of phone, code entries that have vanished can stop access to other accounts. so the screen has to tell three things apart: an empty vault, data that has not loaded yet, and an unsupported transfer. a new phone counts as ready not after a general sync mark, but after the owner has tested the sign-in methods they need.
reconcile the archive after the move

over the years a vault gathers more than usernames and passwords. next to them there can be notes and photos of documents, useful at the moment the entry is opened. a move that kept only the main fields can therefore look finished before the person discovers what is missing.

the import has to work on the device the person actually has. instructions to install an extension on a computer help the owner of a single iphone very little. it matters to name the source formats supported in advance, and to keep separately the pieces for which the new vault has no suitable field.

the way out of a vault matters as much as the way in. if only the old app understands the export, hundreds of entries have to be moved by hand. passwords, notes and attachments should be checked as different parts of the archive: support for the main fields does not yet guarantee that the documents beside them come across.
test your own devices and sign-in methods

a manager is used inside a particular setup: a phone, a browser, a work computer, the connection available. a feature can suit you at home and turn out to be awkward where an extension cannot be installed. passkeys add actions of their own for creating, saving and then signing in.

a break on one platform can make the whole vault awkward. a person keeps the data on a phone but signs in from a work computer; a missing extension or missing passkey support will stop exactly that crossing. capabilities have to be described for particular devices and sign-in methods, not with one blanket “works everywhere”.

a passkey is a separate way in, not one more password line. an app can read the file perfectly well and still be unable to save a key from the service you need. choosing your own cloud will not fix that: sign-in support and the storage place are different decisions, and each has to be described precisely.
help family with boundaries you can see
separate shared from private

a shared entry is useful to a family when everyone involved has the same current version. passing copies around gradually raises the question of who changed the password last and where the right one is now. a shared vault has to keep a clear division between the shared material and each person’s private part.

helping a family member and access in an exceptional situation call for different agreements. ordinary help needs no more than the entries you pick; wider access has to be agreed separately. let people see who is involved and who is responsible for updates, then run a familiar action through together, without handing over a whole private archive for the sake of one sign-in.

a shared database has to stay one current history of changes. when a husband and wife end up with copies that differ, it is unclear where the right password is now. that is the everyday job of sharing; opening the archive in an emergency, after the owner’s illness or death, calls for a procedure of its own and must not be switched on unnoticed along with ordinary sharing.
save the entry that was actually updated
understand why the sign-in was refused
move from a warning to an action
test the second step on the new device
reconcile the archive after the move
test your own devices and sign-in methods
separate shared from private
pick a narrow stretch, not a new vault

the clearest opportunity in these reviews is helping with the move between particular vaults: showing compatibility in advance, carrying the supported parts across and naming what was left out. but even a tool like that works with secrets, so it cannot be treated as a simple file converter. before building the product you need competence in protecting data and a clear answer for temporary copies, errors and the deletion of material.

for a team without that preparation i would not choose a password manager as a first product. improving the interface of an existing, proven solution may make more sense. the value of the move itself can first be judged on a synthetic archive and by watching the current process: where a person gets stuck and what they have to restore by hand.

translator.name: translators
translator.summary: finishing a line, hearing the answer, reading a sign and getting the whole document. how to judge a translator by a job seen through to the end.
body:
one person is trying to explain a request through a phone; the other is waiting for an answer. the translator cuts in too early — and the conversation has to start over. on a trip a similar stop happens because a voice mode is unavailable; in messaging, because a draft was lost. even a good translation of a single phrase does not make up for a break like that.

so several different products hide under the name “translator”. a family conversation needs turns; a trip needs languages available in advance; a document needs the original kept and the gaps visible. below we work through what has to be seen to the end in each case.
talking with someone close
the two people use one phone or a pair of earbuds. both want to finish a thought and understand the answer without learning the settings in the middle of the conversation.
explaining yourself on a trip
what is needed is a sign, an address or a short request in an unfamiliar place. it matters to know in advance what will work without a steady internet connection.
sending a message or reading a document
the writer edits a short message, the reader works through a long file. both need access to the original text, but the volume and the way of checking differ sharply.
understanding each other in a conversation
letting a person finish a thought

an automatic dialogue frees people from constant tapping, as long as it gets the boundaries of a turn right. if the translation starts while someone is speaking, the two of them hear overlapping voices and have to repeat the thought. a manual button gives a different kind of control — the person ends the recording themselves.

when the automatic mode cuts a person off, ending the turn by hand gives them control back. recording, translating and playback have to be distinguishable: it should be clear whether the phone is listening or already answering. that lets two people use one device without voices overlapping.

a short pause does not always mean “i have finished”. long speech needs a different mode: keep recording and leave the earlier fragments available to read. that can help someone listening to a lecture, but it has to be tested separately from turn-taking conversation — lag and errors build up differently there.
checking both directions of the conversation

support for a language has to answer several specific questions: is text available, is voice recognized, and does the reverse direction work. for a conversation with a spouse, translating text is no substitute for the expected ability to speak, even if the language is there in the general list.

a language in the general list does not mean conversation is supported. a person needs to see straight away what their own pair can do: text, speech recognition, playback and the reverse direction. if voice is unavailable, typing can be a fallback way to communicate, but not a replacement for the feature promised before the purchase.

both directions being technically available does not yet make them equally usable. here the user is happy with the translation one way and unhappy with the other. a narrow product for a community has to be tested in a real exchange of lines. everyday cards for care work are an even more specialized scenario: important questions about health cannot be entrusted to an unverified automatic wording.
hearing the phrase you need and repeating it

a translation still has to be heard. speech that is too fast makes it hard to repeat, an unpleasant voice makes the conversation awkward, and playback that is unavailable leaves the person who needs a word’s pronunciation with no answer. the quality of the text and the usability of the audio result should be considered separately.

playback can be too fast even when the translation on the screen is clear. a repeat and a speed control help make out a phrase or say it yourself. on a trip these actions have to be available right next to the result, without going into the general settings list.

in a noisy place a quick repeat without a new recording helps. the playback speed for understanding and the speed for saying something yourself can differ. a saved setting should belong to the chosen language, so that every conversation does not begin with hunting for the control.
keeping the language variant you chose

the name of a language can hide several variants of pronunciation and usage. for talking in a particular place, what matters is the variant chosen, not the general label. a setting that is hard to reach forces a person to work out every time what should have been settled in advance.

a regional label means something if it changes the result and not just the name in a menu. for someone in a particular part of mexico, what matters is words the other person understands. a set of familiar everyday situations with native speakers will show up such differences better than a general judgment on a whole language.

a regional preference should be visible in the mode currently in use. if the camera or the voice does not support the same variant, the difference has to be shown plainly. keeping the choice honestly where that is possible matters more than formally stretching one label across different results.
preparing for a place without the usual connection
testing translation without a connection in advance

a downloaded language and working without a connection are different things, and they have to be tested together. on a trip a weak connection can delay the answer, and the local mode you were counting on can turn out to be unavailable for the action you need. finding that out on the spot is inconvenient, especially after paying separately for access.

preparation should end with a translation that works with the network switched off. text, voice and camera are tested separately: a downloaded pack may serve only some of the modes. the result of that trial matters more than a download badge, because on the trip there may no longer be a convenient way to fix the setting.

the terms of offline access have to be shown before the download and before payment: which languages and which modes the pack includes. the word “offline” creates an expectation immediately. even a feature that technically works will disappoint if the person learns about a paid restriction only just before the trip.
matching the translation to the sign it came from

live translation helps match a sign to where it is right now. that matters when choosing an item on another screen: a separate photo with the text rearranged makes you match them up by hand. for unhurried reading of a photograph, a mode like that can be perfectly sufficient.

these jobs should be told apart before the camera starts. in a moving view what matters is refreshing and keeping the link to where the sign is; in a photo, an easy way back to the original and to individual lines. testing a particular screen or document shows which method actually helps you work it out.

for reading on the move, lag itself becomes the obstacle: the person has already moved the camera while the caption still belongs to the previous frame. for a document you can stop at a photo and check the lines against each other. the choice of mode should depend on that job, not on which effect looks more convincing in a demonstration.
keeping the whole meaning of what was written
keeping the original message until it is sent

translation inside a conversation cuts down on switching between apps. but it has to preserve the usual control over the message: delete a character, fix a phrase, wait for the result and send exactly the text that was chosen. losing the whole draft while editing destroys whatever the built-in keyboard gained.

half a minute of waiting changes the rhythm of the exchange: by the time the translation is ready, a short line may no longer be relevant. while the processing runs, the original has to stay available. the person has to understand what is being translated right now and whether they can carry on editing without losing what they typed.

ordinary editing of a message has to stay ordinary: delete a character, bring back something wiped by accident, carry on typing. if the translation takes time, a result that arrives later must not overwrite a draft that has already been changed. keeping the original is more useful here than one more quick-translate button.
seeing the whole volume and the gaps that are left

a short phrase, a long message and a scanned document call for different routes. a length limit can leave half the text unprocessed, and the absence of import can stop you even starting on a pdf. at the same time, translating a difficult old document can be useful, even though some elements stay in the original.

what is needed is a clear limit before the start and a way to tell the finished parts from the untranslated ones. the original should be kept next to the result, so you can go back to a gap or a name. finishing means understanding the state of the whole document, not the appearance of the first translated paragraph.

a pdf needs a way into the job: pick the file from the folder you are used to, see the pages and understand which parts are supported. if there is no import, the person never even gets as far as checking the translation. after processing, that same page-by-page overview helps find the scans, tables and fragments that were left untranslated.
letting a person finish a thought
checking both directions of the conversation
keeping the language variant you chose
testing translation without a connection in advance
keeping the original message until it is sent
seeing the whole volume and the gaps that are left
one conversation, one language pair

for a first product i would choose regular everyday communication between two people on a single language pair. a job like that makes the whole exchange visible: one has finished a line, the other has heard a translation they understand and replied. before building, you need to check with native speakers whether the quality of the available recognition and playback is good enough. convenient turn-taking will not fix a bad translation.

if the quality holds up, the advantage is worth looking for in control of the conversation: an explicit change of sides, correcting what was heard, repeating the answer and saving the phrases you need. lectures, documents and communication in care work need testing of their own and different limits. it is too early to add them for the sake of the number of modes — first there has to be a conversation the two people were actually able to finish.

astronomy-stargazing.name: night sky and astronomy
astronomy-stargazing.summary: identify the object overhead and prepare an evening with the telescope. what you need to know before going outside, and what helps you keep observing.
body:
a person notices a bright dot and raises their phone to the sky. another plans a trip out with a telescope well in advance. a third wants to see a comet they have only just heard about. each needs a different result: a name, a workable plan for the evening, or a specific object in the catalog.

the number of stars on the map answers none of those requests on its own. what matters is tying the screen to the place, the time and what the observer is able to do. what follows looks at where that link helps, where it breaks, and what separate products can be built on it.
first time looking at the sky with family
the job is to name a visible star or find the moon together with a child. the first object that makes sense matters more than a large catalog and a long acquaintance with the settings.
preparing an evening with the telescope
the observer picks targets, an hour and equipment. a mistake in the preparation burns the limited time outside and can wreck a shared viewing.
looking for a specific event
the person installed the app for a comet or an arrangement of planets. they want to know whether the event can be seen from where they are, and when it makes sense to look.
line the map up with the sky overhead
work out which way the map is pointed

the map makes sense once a person lines it up with what they can see. simple pointing and the name of an object give a quick first success. if the screen shows a different direction, a beginning observer has no idea whether they got it wrong themselves, whether the right place is selected, or whether the device needs configuring.

a star’s name is useful when it is clear which dot it belongs to. if the screen shows no clear link to where you are looking, a newcomer does not know whether to go hunting for a compass setting, change the place, or pick a different object. the first screen should answer exactly that question; the complicated modes can wait.

a familiar visible landmark, the moon for instance, helps check the direction. the map’s place and time have to sit beside it: an accidental jump into the past can look like a pointing error. for a moving dot that check matters even more, but finding a satellite is a separate job that depends on current data, not on confidently naming any object in the sky.
get a short answer about the moon

a question about the moon phase often needs no exploration of the whole map. a person wants to open the app and see the name, the picture of the phase and the date they need straight away. when the label disappears in favor of complicated navigation, a short useful action turns into a search through the interface.

a short answer still has its conditions: the date and time have to match the chosen place. a calendar that is off by a day makes a simple screen unreliable. and personal notes about fishing or other pursuits have to be told apart from astronomical data: a reviewer’s experience does not prove that the phase affects the outcome.

if someone needs the time of the full moon, it should be findable directly by the name of the event. adding the chosen date to a personal calendar grows naturally out of that short job. a big map is not required: a small calendar can be more convenient, as long as it keeps its labels clear and does not bury people in reminders.
prepare a specific observation
find the event you came for

installing the app for a specific event creates a precise expectation: the object has to be findable by name and tied to the place and time of the observation. if it is not there after a themed pack has been bought, the number of other objects does not make up for the chance that was missed.

how current the catalog is gets tested by the name the person came for. before buying a pack they should be able to find the comet they want and see what information about it is available. otherwise dozens of other objects do nothing to finish the one job that caused the install.

there is a difference between an object being absent and an extra charge for showing it. those terms are better set out on the event card before the purchase. a saved plan should lead to the same object for the chosen place and show any corrections if the information has changed.
pick an hour and see the uncertainty

one verdict for the evening hides the differences between hours and conditions. what matters to an observer is when the clouds will arrive, what temperature to expect and what that means for getting the gear ready. a good general forecast can be a useful reference point, but a particular trip out needs a finer reading by time.

the conditions have to refer to the chosen place and show when they were updated. a handsome overall score cannot hide a disagreement with the rain outside the window. separate figures for cloud cover and other conditions help show what the verdict rests on, though on their own they do not make the forecast infallible.

an overall score for the evening can hide clouds arriving at exactly the hour you head out. an hour-by-hour view shows which time the forecast refers to and which figure is changing. it does not remove forecast error, but it gives the observer grounds to move the trip or pick a different target.
get the telescope ready before the gathering

connecting the telescope easily has value together with a direction on screen that makes sense. the fact of a connection on its own does not help aim the equipment if the pointer is missing or hard to check. a mandatory update outdoors adds another problem: the preparation starts during the observation that was already planned.

a connection is not yet control: the observer needs a visible pointer showing the current direction. if the telescope connects but the crosshair is gone, there is no telling where it is aimed. testing a particular setup has to reach that observable result instead of stopping at a “connected” message.

updates and the readiness of the equipment have to be sorted out before heading out with guests. a repeated demand to install firmware that is already installed can take the whole evening. a prepared list of targets is only useful once that groundwork is in place; for a beginner it is worth adding a few achievable observations and clear expectations of their telescope.
choose what to explore next
understand what the model is showing

the map overhead and a journey through a model of the universe are different experiences. in the first, the job is to find an object from the ground; in the second, to see where it sits in a larger space or to examine its surface. wider coverage and a more detailed model are not the same thing either.

a large number of objects does not mean a detailed surface for each of them. if the planets all look the same, free flight soon stops being exploration. for a product like this it matters more to show a few substantial places and to explain what rests on data and what is there as a stand-in illustration.

the promise to “explore the universe” says little about what you can actually do. one person wants an overview of the galaxy, another the surface of a planet, and a search on a general word can lead nowhere. a trial tour of the scales that are supported explains the product better than a slogan like that.

the sky of a chosen past time is a research interest of its own. that is a different axis of the model: what matters here is the range of dates and the assumptions in the calculation, not how far you can zoom toward a planet. a mode like that is worth testing against the questions of a particular writer or teacher.
reach a first observation before paying

a first experience has to get as far as something concrete: naming a star, finding the moon, or looking at the sky for a chosen time. an ad break after every tap interrupts exactly that trial. an unexpected charge for the step they need leaves a person without an answer as to whether the tool suits them.

a useful trial lets someone finish a small scenario on their own sky and shows the paid capabilities in advance. it does not have to open the whole catalog. its job is to help them see a result and choose how deeply to use the product on the basis of something they actually did.

a paid tier is best continued from what the person has already tried. for one that means more detailed objects, for another a calendar or control of equipment. a complaint about paid information on the moon shows one reviewer’s expectation; it does not establish a general list of features that every product is obliged to give away free.
work out which way the map is pointed
get a short answer about the moon
find the event you came for
pick an hour and see the uncertainty
get the telescope ready before the gathering
understand what the model is showing
help someone through a first evening

for a first product i would pick the beginning telescope owner: help them put together a short list of targets suited to their equipment, their place and their time. that scenario is more concrete than a promise to show the whole universe. it has to be tested on a trip that actually happened: whether the preparation at home worked, whether at least some of the chosen targets were found, and whether the reason for a failure was clear. it matters to tell apart what a beautiful photograph leads you to expect and what is available when you observe with your own eyes.

a catalog of rare events, a historical model and control of complicated equipment can become separate directions. they should not all be added at once. the main result for a first product is more modest: a person had an evening that made sense, kept a record of their observations and knows what to try on the next trip out.

resume-builder.name: resume builders
resume-builder.summary: bring an existing resume across, pick the experience that fits the job and get a readable file. where a builder saves work, and where it makes you start again.
body:
work on a resume starts long before a template is chosen. you have to recall your experience, decide what relates to the job and describe it in your own words. someone with a finished document wants to update a few lines; a beginner wants to work out what to write about at all. the same blank form helps each of them differently.

and for both, the work ends outside the editor: with a document that has been sent and says the right things. so a good-looking template is worth judging alongside the import, the saved versions and the export. losing one important description can cancel out the convenience of every step before it.
add to an existing resume
a new job or project has come along. the person wants to change a few lines while keeping the details of the earlier work.
apply from a phone
there is no computer at hand and the job has already been found. the documents need correcting, the attachments need checking, and they have to go out the usual way.
describe your experience more clearly

the author is stuck on the wording, or is preparing a first resume. what they need is questions and examples that help them recall their own work, not ones that ascribe somebody else’s achievements to them.
first gather the experience and put it in order
carry the experience across with the details intact

when an existing document is carried across, what matters is keeping not only the names of the places someone worked but the details the document was written for. an academic cv and a short resume for an application can run to different lengths. cutting a long history down automatically changes the result itself, even if the new page looks tidy.

when there is no import, an update turns into typing it all again. for a person with a long document that can end the acquaintance with a builder before a template is even chosen. a way in through an existing file should leave the original available and show the sections that came across, rather than forcing a blank form to be filled in from the start.

an academic cv can’t be silently cut down to an ordinary one- or two-page resume. the full material should be kept first, and whatever didn’t fit the chosen layout should be shown. the author can put a compact version together separately — that is an editorial decision about content, not a side effect of the import.

if there is no finished document yet, another way in is needed: questions about studies, projects, side jobs and the person’s own contribution. a sample wording helps to start, but it only becomes real experience once the author has made it specific.
choose the order for a particular application

updating a resume is a job in its own right. having added recent work, the person wants it above the earlier one; for another application earlier experience may matter more. if the order is bound rigidly to when things were typed in, a simple edit turns into deleting and retyping the whole history.

moving an entry up is a simple operation, and it should leave its content alone. deleting earlier jobs for the sake of a new order is particularly absurd in a document a person returns to for years. the editor needs explicit actions for reordering, and an undo, rather than an order set by accident at the time of entry.

reordering sections helps present the same experience in different ways. the main archive holds the details; the version for a posting holds the part that was chosen and its order. a hidden project shouldn’t be deleted from the archive, and changing a color or the margins shouldn’t change what the author decided to tell.
see what changed in the wording

a shorter cover letter is a clear benefit of ai. but shortening loses its point if the paragraph breaks off, a detailed job title turns into a generic name, and there is no way back to the original. smooth language can hide the loss of a substantial fact.

a shortened job title can lose the specialization, and skill ratings placed automatically can add a claim that wasn’t in the original. changes like that need showing next to the previous text. the author should accept them piece by piece, keeping the option of going back to the original.

a prompt is useful as a question: what task did the person carry out, what were they responsible for, what result can they back up. ready-made examples help recall the work, but they shouldn’t automatically become achievements. if there is no fact or figure, it is better to leave the author with the question than to fill the gap with a convincing phrase.
change the layout without losing the text

a template should change how the text is presented while leaving the text itself alone. otherwise trying a layout on becomes a risky operation: the person checks whether the name, the place of work or a whole section has disappeared. a similar problem comes up with the letter, when what was written is quietly replaced by the original sample.

if a template doesn’t have room for the name or the experience, that should be visible before it is applied. the chosen layout has to show exactly what doesn’t fit, and the content has to survive independently of it. then a different look for the document can be picked without retyping the sections that were lost.

the cover letter and the sample text should be stored separately too. going back to the template can’t replace a personal draft with somebody else’s words. a history of edits and an independent archive of experience make it possible to return to the last version even after a layout try-on went wrong.
get a document that can actually be sent
know the terms for the finished file in advance

the price of downloading belongs to a builder’s main result. finding out about it after an entire career has been typed in is quite a different experience from choosing a paid export in advance. the same goes for the watermark: a document can be visible in the editor and still not be fit to send as received.

before a big piece of work it is worth finding out which file the chosen access includes, how many times it can be obtained and what changes after payment. a plain layout with no watermark can be enough; a rich catalog of templates is no substitute for clear terms for getting your own document.

a limit on the number of exports makes the preview especially important. a mistake in a template shouldn’t use up an attempt while the person is looking for a description that disappeared. a one-off export and a subscription for regular work on applications are different offers; terms of access to your own text after payment are needed in both cases.
find and open the file after exporting

generating the file, saving it and sending it are different actions. a message about preparing a pdf doesn’t yet mean the document has appeared in a folder you can reach. and a mail button that has been pressed is no confirmation that anything was attached to it.

the person should see a result, not an endless “generating”. once it has been created successfully, the file can be opened, a place to save it can be chosen, and it can be obtained again without rebuilding the resume. if the processing ended in an error, the data that was entered stays where it is and the reason isn’t hidden behind a screen that vanished.

sending the letter is a separate step: a finished file still has to be attached. for one application it helps to put the resume and the cover letter together, showing the recipient and the versions of the attachments. a packet like that helps avoid confusion, but the app has to deliver each file on its own reliably first.
check how it reads outside the editor

the preview shows the template’s intention, while the recipient sees the exported document. characters that have drifted apart, a cover letter with its edge cut off, or a format that wasn’t accepted only turn up after the layout is done. these problems call for different checks: whether the text is complete, where the page ends, and compatibility with a particular way of submitting.

open the finished file outside the builder and look through every page. if it has to be printed, judge that separately. this check answers a practical question: will the person on the other end get the complete, readable document you meant to send.

a file with a pdf extension may still not be accepted by a particular upload form. the limits of the form and a broken document have to be told apart, keeping the option of getting another suitable version. checking that the text can be extracted will also show the reading order; it predicts neither the employer’s decision nor getting through every screening system.
carry the experience across with the details intact
choose the order for a particular application
see what changed in the wording
change the layout without losing the text
find and open the file after exporting
check how it reads outside the editor
carry one update through to sending

for a first product i would choose a person who already has a resume and needs to prepare a new application quickly. that is a definite job: bring the document across, add recent experience, pick out what relates to the posting and get a file. on a real resume you can see clearly how much typing was removed and whether important details went missing.

the priority is keeping the content and a separate version for a posting. new templates and generated wording make sense after that. helping a beginner with a first resume is a promising hypothesis too, but it calls for a different way in, through questions. joining both scenarios in one long form isn’t worth it: it makes an experienced author repeat themselves and still doesn’t explain to a beginner what to write about.

music-streaming.name: listening to music
music-streaming.summary: the queue, the library and where you stopped: why a listener needs their own choices to survive, even when they change device or music service.
body:
sometimes you want to hear something new; sometimes you want exactly the album you already picked. those intentions are easy to mix up: recommendations push into the queue, a rare version disappears from the list, a long mix starts over. the person is operating the app again instead of listening.

the reviews contain requests aimed at several different products: a player for personal files, a tool for moving a collection, and conversation around music. the shared motive is keeping your own choices. what follows looks at where they get lost, without treating every improvement as a reason to build yet another streaming service.
building a collection of their own
this listener picks particular editions, keeps rare files and remembers the order of the albums. losing a list means losing accumulated work, even if the songs can still be found.
listening on the move
the music is chosen in advance and the connection can drop. the queue has to carry on after a stop, without hunting for tracks on screen again.
looking for music and people to talk to
one wants new performances of a familiar work, another a station in their own language, a third an exchange of impressions with friends. these are different ways of coming back to music.
choose the familiar or find something new
keep the boundaries you set for the queue

shuffling the songs you saved and adding similar ones are two different instructions. in the first, the person has already set the boundaries of the choice. repeats from a small part of the collection, or a sudden genre from elsewhere, make that choice pointless: you end up watching the player and skipping tracks.

shuffle should change the order inside the list you chose. when the same sequence comes back on every start, the listener does not get the variety they expected, even though the mode is formally on. a visible queue helps you see what comes next and change the selection without rebuilding the collection.

recommendations need consent of their own. sometimes a person is ready to step outside the list, sometimes they want to stay inside a genre or an album. a dislike should have a clear effect on what gets picked, and turning suggestions down should leave the queue already chosen intact. this is an improvement to an existing player, not in itself a reason for a new music service.
give a discovery somewhere to go

a good discovery is not necessarily a song that resembles the last one. you can arrive at it through a composer you do not know, a small artist, a mood or a curated radio station. the value comes from recordings sitting next to each other in a way that is unexpected but makes sense: you start wondering where else this choice leads.

give a discovery somewhere to go: save the track, open the artist, return to the selection. a curated station and a catalog search can coexist, because they ask for different degrees of involvement. for someone who loves rare music, the breadth within a familiar genre can matter more than the size of the catalog overall.

a curated station offers a character of selection that people want to come back to. that differs from an algorithmic search for a similar song. for some people that entrance is classical music with a choice of performance, for others a broadcast in a familiar language. both directions need their own audience and an available source of music.
understand what went into the history

listening history helps a person see their own musical year: which songs carried a month, what they kept coming back to, what unexpectedly became a favorite. for that job a counter is a way of remembering, and sorting by play count is another way into the collection.

explain the period and what the figure covers right next to it. a monthly total, daily activity and the full history answer different questions. looking at one chart should not turn into a separate journey through advertising: a short return to familiar music loses its point if it takes too many steps.

sorting by play count is another way of opening up a personal collection. at the same time the product has to explain which data went into the counter and over what period. a diary of impressions can fill out an incomplete history, but it must not pass personal marks off as exact statistics from every service.
agree on who picks the next recording

listening at the same time as someone close and meeting someone through shared taste are different social jobs. in a shared session it is already known who is taking part; what remains is agreeing on the queue and on the controls. when meeting someone, you first have to make sense of another person’s taste and decide whether you want to start talking.

in listening together it is already known who the person wants to be with. the problem is a different one: joining, seeing the shared queue and working out who controls it. a connection failure wrecks the meeting, even if matching people by taste in the same app works well.

finding people with similar taste can be a reason to buy on its own. removing a feature like that leaves a person without the activity they paid for, even if the player keeps playing. for a diary shared with friends you first have to understand whether people value the conversation, each other’s recommendations, or specifically meeting new people: those are different reasons to come back.
keep your own music library
keep the contents even when a track disappears

a playlist holds decisions that are hard to repeat from memory: which recording to choose, what to put next to it, what to leave for later. that is why a list disappearing is not the same as one track being temporarily unavailable. the order a person assembled is lost, even though the songs themselves still exist.

keep the contents of a collection separately from whether it can be played. an entry for an unavailable song is more useful than an empty slot: from it you can find another version or rebuild the list. before changing device or moving between services it matters to see which selections came across in full and which need attention.

losing a local collection after the app is offloaded is a separate case: the names, the order and the files themselves can be stored in different ways. before freeing up space a person needs to see what will remain and how to get the rest back. moving between services adds a check of track versions: a matching title does not yet mean the same recording.
tell your own files apart from access to them

personal music files offer another way to assemble a library: keep your own recordings and rare versions, organize them on a computer and carry on listening from the phone. that route is especially valuable when the work you want is not in the usual catalog, or when its availability has changed.

convenience is decided by the whole chain from storage to playback. test the formats of your files, the order of the albums and access to the recordings you want on the phone. a stream from a home server and a local copy solve different jobs; the collection screen should help tell them apart instead of making you guess from the play button.

a streaming catalog can change after a move to another country: the service you are used to, or a recording, turns out to be unavailable. personal files are another way to assemble a library, provided a person has suitable recordings and the right to use them. but a new player should not promise to bring back a blocked catalog; it is responsible for the files the owner has and for the order they were kept in.
carry on listening somewhere else
carry on listening after a stop

a download badge is only useful when the music you chose is genuinely available on the trip you need it for. what matters is what the downloaded selection contains and on what terms it is stored. a track that has appeared in the list still has to be told apart from a track ready to play with no connection.

in the car the queue carrying on is added to that: after a short stop you want to hear the next track you chose. test a familiar trip with a stop and a return. if the controls in the car show one choice while something else is playing, large buttons do not fix the main problem, the loss of control over listening.

after a stop or a reconnection the queue should stay where it was. for a long mix the exact position is added to that: hunting for it again is awkward. this is a possible specialization for a player built around long recordings, but reviews about a car queue that vanished do not on their own prove demand for a separate app for mixes.
know what a setting has been applied to

sound settings become a personal part of the collection: the right equalizer lets someone hear music the way the owner of a particular pair of headphones likes it. but a change that helps one track can get in the way of the next. that difference shows up most with playback speed and with individual presets.

show the scope beside the setting: the current recording, the selection you chose, or the whole player. after a preset is switched, the position of the controls should match the state that is applied. being able to go back to the original sound quickly helps compare changes without memorizing every move of a slider.

playback speed needs a scope that is clear: this track only, or the whole player. otherwise a setting made for one performance changes the next by accident. a home system adds another choice, a particular speaker or room. controlling it belongs to the hardware and calls for a check of its own, not simply one more equalizer tab.
give a discovery somewhere to go
understand what went into the history
keep the contents even when a track disappears
tell your own files apart from access to them
carry on listening after a stop
know what a setting has been applied to
keep the collection, do not build a whole streaming service

for a small team i would first test backing up and transferring playlists between a specific set of supported services. the result here is clear: the person sees the order they had, the recordings that are unavailable and the matches that look doubtful. before any development you have to be sure the services permit, and technically allow, getting the data you need. without that a handsome transfer screen will not become a working product.

the alternative is a player for people who own their files, with one good scenario for the road and offline access. a music diary and home audio call for a different audience and different reasons to come back. it is not worth combining everything at once: the initial advantage should preserve one particular collection or habit of the listener, rather than promise to replace their whole musical life.
